questions.q: A cold room logs its temperature every minute. Food safety wants the longest stretch of consecutive minutes during which the temperature stayed below 5 °C, allowing at most two readings above it (sensor glitches). Which pattern fits?
questions.explain: "Longest stretch of consecutive" is a contiguous range of variable length. The window's summary is the number of readings above 5 °C; shrink from the left while it exceeds 2. It is the on-time streak problem with a different story.
options: A variable sliding window that counts the bad readings inside it

questions.q: Two carts must be compared: do they contain the same products in the same quantities, in any order? Which pattern fits best?
questions.explain: "Same items, any order" depends only on counts. One table, O(n + m) time. Sorting both carts would also work, in O(n log n).
options: Frequency counter: count up for one cart, down for the other

questions.q: Product prices are sorted ascending. Count the pairs of different products whose total fits a ₦20,000 gift card. Which pattern gives O(n)?
questions.explain: Sorted data and a question about pairs. When prices[left] + prices[right] fits, all right − left partners of left fit at once; otherwise right is too expensive for anyone and moves in.
options: Two pointers from both ends: if the ends fit, the left item fits with everything up to the right one

questions.q: An e-bike route has charging stops at known distances. What is the smallest battery range that completes the route charging at most 4 times? Which pattern fits?
questions.explain: "The smallest value such that…" with a monotonic check: a bigger battery never needs more charges. It is the truck-capacity search in another costume.
options: Binary search on the answer, with "can the route be done with this range and at most 4 charges?" as the check
Two pointers on the stop list

questions.q: A dashboard lets thousands of managers ask for total sales between any two dates of the past year. The daily figures do not change. What should you build?
questions.explain: Arbitrary, unrelated ranges over static data are exactly what prefix sums are for: O(n) once, O(1) per query.
options: A prefix-sum array, built once; each query is one subtraction
A frequency table of sales amounts
A binary search per query over the amounts

questions.q: Net cash flow per day can be negative. You need the number of periods whose total is exactly ₦0. Why not a shrinking sliding window?
questions.explain: A range from i to j totals 0 exactly when the running totals before i and at j are equal. Counting equal running totals is a frequency count.
options: With negative values a window's total can go down as it grows, so there is no safe moment to shrink; prefix sums with a Map of earlier prefix sums work instead
A sliding window would be O(n²)

questions.q: A reservoir's level only ever falls during a drought. Given the daily levels, find the first day it drops below the safe level. Which approach is fastest?
questions.explain: A monotonic yes/no over positions: the first true is the answer, in O(log n). Sorting would destroy the day order you need.
options: Binary search over the days: "below the safe level on day d" is false, then true

questions.q: Transactions arrive one by one from a webhook. You must report two that sum to a refund as soon as both have arrived. Why is a Map better than two pointers here?
questions.explain: The pattern follows the constraints: complete and sorted data suits two pointers; streaming, unsorted data suits a lookup table.
options: Two pointers need the complete list, sorted; a stream is neither, while a Map answers "have I seen the other half?" in O(1) at each arrival
Two pointers cannot handle kobo amounts

questions.q: A nightly job compares the 25 items of two small lists with a nested loop. A reviewer asks you to replace it with a frequency counter. What is the best response?
questions.explain: Patterns earn their complexity on large inputs or hot paths. Asking "how big is the input, and how often does this run?" comes before choosing a pattern.
options: At 25 items the nested loop does at most a few hundred comparisons once a night; keep the simpler code unless the lists will grow

questions.q: A radio station must split a day's ads (in order, with durations) into 6 consecutive blocks, making the longest block as short as possible. Which earlier problem is this?
questions.explain: "Split into k consecutive groups, minimise the largest" is always the same search: check a limit greedily in O(n), and binary search the limit between the longest ad and the total.
options: The minimum truck capacity (and splitting a route between riders): binary search on the longest block allowed
The longest block without a repeated ad

questions.q: For "the shortest span of events that includes every warehouse", what summary does the sliding window keep?
questions.explain: The counts let you update when an event leaves; the "covered" number tells you in O(1) whether the window is valid, without checking every warehouse each step.
options: The total of the minutes inside
A count per warehouse inside the window, plus how many required warehouses have a count above zero
Only the first and last event
A sorted copy of the window

questions.q: In the shortest-cover window, when does left move?
questions.explain: For "shortest valid", shrink while valid. For "longest valid" (like the on-time streak), shrink only while invalid.
options: Only when the window is invalid
While the window is valid: record its span, then drop the leftmost event to try a shorter one

questions.q: Managers try hundreds of starting-stock values against the same 90-day sales plan. Why prefix sums plus binary search, instead of scanning the plan for each value?
questions.explain: Precompute once, query many times. The precondition (no negative sales) is what makes the running totals monotonic.
options: The running totals are built once in O(n); each query is then O(log n) instead of O(n), and running totals never decrease, so binary search is valid
Binary search needs less memory than scanning

questions.q: For the longest balanced card/cash run, the Map stores the first position of each running balance and never updates it. Why?
questions.explain: For counting ranges you need how many times each balance appeared; for the longest range you need where it first appeared. Same table idea, different question.
options: A later position with the same balance could only give a shorter range; the earliest one gives the longest
Because the balance is always positive

questions.q: Traffic data is not sorted, yet binary search finds a peak minute. What justifies discarding half?
questions.explain: Binary search needs a proof that the answer is on one side, not sorted data. Here the proof comes from comparing neighbours.
options: If the next minute is busier than the middle, a peak must exist to the right (values either keep rising to the end or fall after a top); otherwise one exists at the middle or to its left
Peaks are always in the middle
It is a guess that usually works

questions.q: The "two orders within 10 minutes" check keeps only each customer's most recent order. What must be true of the input?
questions.explain: Sort or buffer late events first, or compare against every order in the last 10 minutes. The logic was right; the precondition was not.
options: Customers must be sorted by name
Orders must arrive in time order; a late event is compared with the wrong "previous" order and real pairs are missed
Each customer must have at most two orders

questions.q: In a coding interview you are given a problem statement. What should you do first?
questions.explain: The constraints decide the pattern: "sorted?" chooses two pointers over a Map; "streaming?" rules out two pointers; "negative values?" rules out a shrinking window.
options: Ask clarifying questions: input size, sortedness, duplicates, edge cases, what to return when there is no answer

questions.q: You solved pair-sum with a Map. The interviewer adds: "the list is sorted and you may not allocate extra memory". What now?
questions.explain: Changing plan when constraints change, and saying why the new approach is correct, is exactly what the follow-up is testing.
options: Keep the Map; it is still O(n)
Switch to two pointers from both ends: O(n) time, O(1) space, correct because each move discards an amount that cannot be in any pair
Use binary search for every element, O(n²)

questions.q: Any peak is a correct answer, so the fast and brute-force versions may return different peaks. How does the harness still test findPeak?
questions.explain: When several answers are valid, test the property every valid answer has. Comparing with one reference answer would fail correct code.
options: It checks the fast answer against the definition (busier than its neighbours) instead of comparing it with one particular answer
It compares only the first element

questions.q: Why does the harness stop at the first disagreement and print the input?
questions.explain: Keeping generated inputs small (a dozen items) means the first failure is usually small enough to trace. The lesson also runs a deliberately broken version, so you know the harness can fail.
options: A small failing input is the most useful thing a test can give: you can trace it by hand to find the bug
Because later inputs are always correct

questions.q: To offer the 3 free delivery slots closest to 14:10 from a sorted list of slots, which combination is most efficient?
questions.explain: O(log n + k) instead of O(n log n). The closest slots are always next to the insertion point, on one side or the other.
options: Sort all slots by distance from 14:10
Binary search for where 14:10 would go, then two pointers moving outwards, taking the closer side each time
A fixed-size sliding window over the whole list
A frequency counter of slot times

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Running balances: −1, 0, 1, 0, 1, 2. Balance 0 first appears "before" the start (−1) and again at position 3, giving length 4 (cash, card, card, cash). Balance 1 first appears at 2 and again at 4, giving only 2.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The shortest stretch containing A, B and C has 3 events: B, A, C (positions 1 to 3) or A, C, B (positions 2 to 4).

questions.q: The window wraps around the end of the week. What does this print?
questions.explain: The windows starting at positions 0 to 5 total 10, 12, 20, 16, 14 and 6. The quietest one starts at position 5 and wraps: 0 + 5 + 1 = 6. Without wrapping it would have been missed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: By the end of day 2, 80 units are sold, so a stock of 80 runs out on day 2 and 81 on day 3. 200 units outlast the plan, which only sells 140.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For the first list the middle (4) is followed by 5, so the search goes right and ends at 6 (position 4), although 9 at position 1 is also a peak: any peak is allowed. A rising list peaks at the end, a falling one at the start.

questions.q: Split the stops between 2 riders so the busiest carries as little as possible. What does this print?
questions.explain: At a limit of 18: 7 + 2 + 5 = 14 (adding 10 would exceed), then 10 + 8 = 18, so 2 riders. At 17 the second rider cannot take both 10 and 8, so a third is needed.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The merge always takes the smaller head, so the output is sorted, and an id equal to the last one written is skipped: each 3 is written once.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A (500) and B (700) find no partner. C (300) finds B (700). D (500) finds A, because A's 500 was stored; a second 500 is not stored again, so the first id is kept.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Every stretch of 4 views touches 3 categories. The longest with at most 2 have 3 views: shoes, bags, shoes; shoes, hats, hats; or hats, hats, bags.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first slot at or after 730 is 760, at position 3. 700 and 760 are both 30 minutes away; on a tie the earlier slot is taken first, then 760 beats 660.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The running totals are 0 (before the start), 2, 0, 3, 0, 0. Each pair of equal running totals is one zero-sum period: the value 0 appears four times, giving 6 pairs.

questions.q: Print the length of the longest stretch of consecutive views touching at most 2 categories, then at most 3. Use a variable sliding window with a Map of counts.
questions.explain: Add each view to the counts; while more than maxCategories categories are inside, remove from the left and delete categories whose count reaches 0, so counts.size stays accurate. O(n) time.

questions.q: Print three different payouts (as a sorted array) that add up to ₦25,000, or null, in better than O(n³). Then try ₦1,000.
questions.explain: Sort a copy, then for each payout run the two-pointer pair search on the ones after it. O(n²) time. 6,000 + 8,000 + 11,000 is the first triple the walk reaches.

questions.q: Prices are sorted. Count the pairs whose prices differ by exactly the given amount, using two pointers moving in the same direction (O(n)). Prices are distinct.
questions.explain: For each i, advance j while the difference is too small; since both only move forward, the total work is O(n). A Set of prices (look up price + diff) also works in O(n) time with O(n) space.

questions.q: Print the day (starting at 1) on which the stock runs out for starting stocks of 350, 351 and 5,000 units, or null if it lasts the whole plan. Build running totals, then binary search them.
questions.explain: Running totals are 120, 200, 350, 450, …; the first day whose total reaches the stock is the run-out day. 350 units are exactly used up on day 3; 351 last into day 4.

questions.q: Print the length (number of events) of the shortest stretch of pick events that includes every required warehouse, or 0 if none does.
questions.explain: A variable window with counts per warehouse and a "covered" number; shrink while valid, recording lengths. ABJ, LAG, PHC (positions 2 to 4) is the shortest.

questions.q: Print the length of the longest run of consecutive payments with as many card as cash payments. Use running balances (+1 card, −1 cash) and a Map of the first position of each balance.
questions.explain: Start the Map with balance 0 at position −1 so runs starting at the first payment count. Here the whole day is balanced: 4 card, 4 cash.

questions.q: Print the position and value of a peak minute (busier than its neighbours) using binary search, not a scan.
questions.explain: If the next minute is busier, a peak lies to the right; otherwise at the middle or to its left. This search lands on 720 at position 5; 580 at position 2 is also a peak, and either would be correct.

questions.q: Split the stops, in order, between 3 riders so the busiest carries as few parcels as possible, and print that number; then for 1 rider.
questions.explain: Search the limit between the biggest stop (20) and the total (84). At 31: 9 + 14 + 6 = 29, 11 + 20 = 31, 4 + 13 + 7 = 24. At 30 a fourth rider would be needed.
